Q10244: Diwali, or Dipavali, is the Hindu festival of lights, also observed with variations by Jains and Sikhs. It marks the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and falls between about mid-October and mid-November, usually over five or six days. Among the events it recalls is Rama's return to Ayodhya with Sita and Lakshmana.
Q10283: The Kumbh Mela is a Hindu pilgrimage held every four or twelve years, timed by the movement of Jupiter, at four places: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain. The Puranas tell that drops of the nectar of immortality fell at these sites. A Mela lasts one to three months and draws enormous crowds — by Wikipedia's figures, about 660 million people in 2025.
Q1051839: Pashmina is fine cashmere wool from the Changthangi goat — pashm is Persian for ‘wool’ — and, by extension, the Kashmir shawls woven from it. In Kashmir the word meant the raw, unspun wool of these goats. Today ‘pashmina’ can mean either the fibre or the shawl.
Q1057953: Ceviche is a cold dish of raw fish or shellfish cured in citrus juice with seasonings. Versions are eaten along Latin America's Pacific coast, but it is considered Peru's national dish.
Q1071518: Chhau is a semi-classical dance from eastern India that blends martial, acrobatic and folk movement. It survives in three styles named after where they are danced — Purulia in West Bengal, Seraikella in Jharkhand and Mayurbhanj in Odisha — and the Purulia and Seraikella dancers wear masks to show their characters. Its stories come largely from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas.
Q11019445: The Kawagoe Hikawa Festival is held on the third weekend of October in Kawagoe, Saitama Prefecture, and has a history of more than 360 years. Its pageant of floats moves through the old castle town, including the warehouse district of Kurazukuri, and draws around a million visitors. Its float event became a National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 2005.
Q1133754: Timkat is the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo celebration of Epiphany, held on 19 January (20 in a leap year). It commemorates the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan with a ritual re-enactment of baptism. At its centre is the tabot, a model of the Ark of the Covenant kept on every Ethiopian altar, which is carried in procession wrapped in cloth.
Q11435617: Dainichido Bugaku is a yearly set of sacred dances and music held at the Dainichido hall in Kazuno, Akita Prefecture. Tradition says court musicians taught the dances to local people in the early eighth century while the hall was being rebuilt. Seven dances are performed today, accompanied by flute and taiko, with masks including shishi and Vairocana.
Q1165268: The Danza de los Voladores, the ‘dance of the flyers’, is an ancient Mesoamerican ritual still performed in parts of Mexico. Thought to have begun among the Nahua, Huastec and Otomi peoples of central Mexico, it sees five men climb a pole about 30 metres high; four launch themselves off, tied by ropes, and circle down to the ground while the fifth dances and plays flute and drum at the top.
Q1165850: The simsimiyya is a lyre with a box- or bowl-shaped body, played in Egypt since ancient times. Older Egyptian models had five strings held by pegs; many today have twelve. It is central to sawahli, the popular music of Egypt's northern coast.
Q12246208: The Tan-Tan Moussem is a yearly gathering of more than thirty tribes from southern Morocco and other parts of north-west Africa, held in the town of Tan-Tan since 1963. A moussem is a traditional fair with economic, cultural and social roles; this one was founded to promote local traditions and to give people a place to meet, trade and celebrate.
Q140432104: Shantiniketan batik developed at Santiniketan in West Bengal, where Rabindranath Tagore popularised batik. It is hand-painted rather than mechanically printed, using a small brush (tuli) for intricate designs, and is coloured with natural dyes from leaves, bark and other plant materials.
Q1428368: Kente is a Ghanaian textile of narrow hand-woven strips of silk and cotton sewn together, now protected as a geographical indication of Ghana. It was traditionally worn wrapped like a toga by the Asante, Akan and Ewe peoples; Asante tradition places its origin in Bonwire in the Ashanti Region. Today it is worn widely for special occasions.
Q1467960: The mbira is a family of instruments made of a wooden board — often with a resonator — fitted with staggered metal tines that are plucked with the thumbs and fingers. It is traditional to the Shona people of Zimbabwe, and related instruments are played across eastern and southern Africa.
Q15265616: The Passion Play of Iztapalapa, held every Holy Week in a borough of Mexico City, is one of the oldest and best-known passion plays in Mexico. It began not in colonial times but with a procession asking for relief from a 19th-century cholera epidemic. Today it involves hundreds of actors and thousands of ‘Nazarenes’ who carry their own crosses behind the actor playing Jesus.
Q15982556: Hyderabadi haleem is a thick stew of meat, lentils and pounded wheat, slow-cooked to a paste. Haleem is originally an Arab dish; it was brought to Hyderabad State by the Chaush community in the time of the Nizams, and local spices shaped a distinctly Hyderabadi version that was popular by the 20th century. It is especially associated with Ramadan.
Q167067: Ramlila, ‘Rama's play’, is the folk re-enactment of the life of Rama from the Ramayana and works based on it, such as the Ramcharitmanas. Thousands of performances are staged during the autumn festival of Navaratri, building up to Dussehra night, when giant effigies of Ravana are burnt, often with fireworks.
Q1781796: Sega is one of the main music genres of Mauritius and Réunion — a complete performance art of music, storytelling and dance. Its many forms reflect the mixed heritage of the Mauritian people, from modern fusions such as seggae to the drum-led sega tambour of Rodrigues and the Chagos islanders.
Q1810575: Thieboudienne (ceebu jën in Wolof) is Senegal's national dish: fish, broken rice and tomato sauce cooked together in one pot, often with onions, carrots, cabbage, cassava, hot pepper and lime. Related rice dishes are eaten across West and Central Africa, with meat (tiep yappa) or chicken (tiep ganaar) instead of fish.
Q1824110: The Durbar is a yearly religious, cultural and equestrian festival at the heart of Hausa culture in northern Nigeria, with roots going back centuries in the Hausa kingdoms. It is held in the old emirate cities — among them Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, Zazzau, Bauchi, Bida and Ilorin — after Ramadan and at the Eid festivals, with grand processions of horsemen.
Q191000: The oud is a short-necked, pear-shaped, fretless lute of the Middle East, usually strung with eleven strings in six courses. Related instruments, such as the Persian barbat, predate Islam, and the European lute descends from the medieval oud. Distinct versions are played in the Arab world, Turkey and beyond.
Q199701: Kabuki is a classical Japanese theatre that combines drama and dance, known for its stylised acting, lavish costumes and the bold kumadori make-up of some roles. It is traced to Izumo no Okuni's female troupe in early Edo-period Kyoto; after women were banned from the stage in 1629 it became an all-male art, reaching its height in the mid-18th century.
Q21002400: Q'eswachaka is the last surviving Inca rope bridge, made of grass ropes spanning the Apurímac River near Huinchiri in southern Peru. Although a modern bridge stands nearby, families from four local communities rebuild it every year in the second week of June, twisting grass into ropes and cables and laying new decking.
Q22039472: Intore, the ‘dance of heroes’, is a men's dance of Rwanda and Burundi. In pre-colonial times it was a war dance of the Rwandan royal army, performed with real weapons; dancers now carry replicas. Today it is performed at family celebrations, public ceremonies and national events.
Q22304608: Muga is a wild silk of Assam, known for its natural golden-yellow colour, glossy shimmer and great durability; it was once reserved for royalty. It comes from the Assam silkmoth, whose larvae feed on the aromatic leaves of the som and sualu trees in the Brahmaputra Valley. Its lustre is said to grow with every wash.
Q22342962: Stone carving is an ancient craft of Odisha, practised mainly in Puri, Bhubaneswar and Lalitgiri in Cuttack district. Its finest expression is the intricate sculpture of the Sun Temple at Konark. Today's carvers make both commissioned art and everyday objects in stone.
Q2238334: Oku-noto no Aenokoto is a harvest ritual passed down among farming families on the Noto Peninsula in Ishikawa Prefecture. In December the farmer welcomes the god of the rice field into the home with a lantern, in ceremonial dress, and serves it a meal as though the unseen guest — believed to be a family ancestor — were present.
Q22455871: The Thanjavur art plate is a circular plate made only in the Thanjavur region of Tamil Nadu, combining silver, bronze and copper, with figures of Hindu gods and goddesses embossed at its centre.
Q22661954: Santiniketan leather goods are made in Santiniketan and nearby villages in West Bengal from vegetable-tanned sheep and goat leather, decorated by touch dyeing. Its artistic bags are exported to countries including Japan and the United States.
Q22704232: Kutch embroidery is the embroidery tradition of the communities of Kutch district in Gujarat, worked mostly by women on cotton — and sometimes silk or satin — with cotton or silk thread. It uses stitches such as square chain, double buttonhole, darning, running, satin and straight stitch, and sparkles with small mirrors called abhla sewn into the design.
Q22909421: The Tirupati laddu is the sweet given as prasadam at the Venkateswara Temple in Tirumala, Andhra Pradesh. First introduced in 1715, it grew out of an earlier sweet called manoharam and is made in the temple kitchen by more than 600 people, including skilled cooks called pachakas.
Q234138: Washoku, the traditional cuisine of Japan, is built on rice and miso soup with side dishes that follow the seasons — fish, pickled vegetables and vegetables simmered in broth. Seafood may be grilled, served raw as sashimi or sushi, or fried in light tempura batter; noodles such as soba and udon are another staple.
Q2408955: Qoyllur Rit'i, ‘bright white snow’, is a religious festival held each year in the Sinakara Valley of Peru's Cusco Region. It blends Catholic devotion with an Andean celebration of the stars — above all the return of the Pleiades in June, which signals the coming harvest and the new year.
Q24944919: Kashmiri papier-mâché is a craft said to have been brought from Persia in the 14th century by the Sufi saint Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani. Made from paper pulp and richly painted, it takes the form of vases, bowls, boxes, trays, lamp bases and other small objects, made in homes and workshops in Srinagar and across the Kashmir Valley.
Q24945118: Sankheda furniture is teak furniture from Sankheda village, about 45 km from Vadodara in Gujarat, lacquered and painted in traditional shades of maroon and gold. Newer pieces come in many other colours, and the furniture is sold across India and exported to Europe and West Asia.
Q24945749: The Chamba rumal is an embroidered cloth from the former princely state of Chamba in Himachal Pradesh, once promoted under the patronage of its rulers. Worked in bright colours with detailed patterns, it is a customary wedding gift.
Q254093: Tahtib began as an Egyptian martial art of stick fighting and later also became a folk dance with a wooden stick, often performed as mock combat to music. Practised mainly in Upper Egypt, it is regularly performed in Luxor and Aswan. Its original name describes it as the art of being straight and honest through the use of the stick.
Q2624660: Pattachitra is traditional scroll painting on cloth from Odisha, West Bengal and parts of Bangladesh, known for fine detail and for its mythological stories and folk tales. In Odisha it was first made for ritual use and as souvenirs for pilgrims to Puri and other temples; in Bengal, painted scrolls were used to illustrate songs as they were sung.
Q2656133: Kumi odori is a form of narrative dance-theatre from the Ryukyu Kingdom, first presented in the capital, Shuri, in 1719 to entertain Chinese envoys. The courtier Tamagusuku Chokun is credited with establishing it. Drawing on several East Asian dance traditions, it remains part of Okinawan culture today.
Q2723230: The Banarasi sari is woven in Varanasi (Banaras) and is counted among India’s finest saris. It is made of finely woven silk with gold and silver brocade (zari), which makes it comparatively heavy. Its hallmarks include intertwining floral and leaf motifs called kalga and bel, and a row of upright leaves, the jhallar, along the border.
Q2765981: The Baluchari sari is a silk sari from West Bengal, famous for the mythological scenes woven into its end-piece (anchal). Once made in Murshidabad, authentic Baluchari saris are now woven only in and around Bishnupur, and a single sari takes about a week.
Q28154356: Bigwala is the ceremonial gourd-trumpet music and dance of the Busoga Kingdom in Uganda. A solo trumpet is joined by four or more others that build a melody by interlocking single notes (hocketing), then by singers and dancers who circle the players. Once played at royal coronations and funerals, it is now rare, with only a few older masters left.
Q28171926: Manipuri Sankirtana is the ritual singing, drumming and dancing of the Meitei people of Manipur, performed in temples and homes. Through it, performers tell stories of Krishna with intense devotion. It is practised mainly by Vaishnava Meitei Hindus in Manipur and by Manipuri communities in neighbouring Tripura and Assam.
Q2870132: Attiéké is a dish made from fermented, grated cassava pulp, popular in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana; dried, it has a texture like couscous. It is a speciality of the lagoon peoples of southern Côte d'Ivoire — among them the Ebrié, Adjoukrou and Alladjan — and of the Nzema of western Ghana. The name comes from the Ebrié word ‘adjèkè’.
Q2909502: The bolon, or M'Bolon, is a three-stringed harp of Mali and Guinea, made from a large calabash covered in goatskin with a bow-shaped neck. It was played at hunting ceremonies and before battle to give warriors courage. The player holds it between the legs, plucking the strings and striking the calabash like a drum.
Q2961169: Charrería is Mexico's national sport, grown out of the cattle-herding and horsemanship of the haciendas of colonial New Spain. It began as ranch-work contests between haciendas; after the Mexican Revolution, charros who had moved to the cities formed associations to keep their skills alive, and the tradition spread from Jalisco and Hidalgo.
Q309256: The Day of the Dead is celebrated mainly on 1 and 2 November, with some places adding other days. Families and friends gather to remember those who have died, often with humour and stories about them. It is widely observed in Mexico and among people of Mexican heritage elsewhere, and falls during the Christian season of Allhallowtide.
Q3108584: Thanjavur (Tanjore) painting is a classical South Indian painting style from Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu. It draws on the art patronised by the Nayakas of Thanjavur from around 1600, but took the form known today at the Maratha court of Thanjavur (1676–1855). Its subjects are chiefly Hindu deities.
Q3201198: The kôrêdugaw are sacred clowns of Mali, part of secret societies such as the Kore society of the Bambara people. Through deliberately outrageous behaviour — gluttony, mockery and bawdy humour — they teach morality and wisdom, and they also give advice and settle disputes. They perform in the streets, dancing and leading crowds through neighbourhoods.
Q3270102: Bebinca is a layered cake of Indo-Portuguese Goa, often called the queen of Goan desserts. A traditional bebinca has between seven and sixteen layers, each baked in turn. It is especially associated with Christmas, though it is now sold all year.
Q3339328: The Ngondo is a yearly water festival of the Sawa, the coastal peoples of Douala in Cameroon. Its high point is a ceremony on a beach of Wouri Bay, where a devotee enters the water to visit the kingdom of the miengu, mermaid-like water spirits believed to bring good fortune.
Q3349224: The rosogolla, or rasgulla — a ‘syrup-filled ball’ — is a dessert of chhena (fresh cheese) dumplings cooked in light sugar syrup. It is agreed to come from the east of the subcontinent, but its exact birthplace is disputed between West Bengal and Odisha, where it is offered at the Jagannath Temple in Puri. Both states now hold Geographical Indications for their own versions.
Q3363182: The Parachicos are masked dancers of Chiapa de Corzo in Chiapas, who fill the town's streets during the Grand Fiesta from 15 to 23 January each year. The festival honours the town's patron saints — the Black Christ of Esquipulas, Saint Anthony Abbot and Saint Sebastian — and mixes Catholic and Spanish custom with older Indigenous culture.
Q3453150: Congolese rumba is a dance music born in Kinshasa and Brazzaville, the capitals of the two Congos. Sung mostly in Lingala, it is known for its interlocking, cyclical guitar lines, guitar solos and emotive vocals, and has been influential across Africa and beyond.
Q3758080: The gandoura is a light tunic of wool or cotton worn across North Africa and West Asia. In Algeria there are two kinds: a casual hoodless tunic for men, and the women's gandoura, also called the jebba fergani — a ceremonial dress of heavy velvet from the Constantine region.
Q464129: Mariachi is a genre of regional Mexican music that grew up in the countryside of western Mexico from at least the 18th century. A typical group has up to eight violins, two trumpets and guitars — including the high vihuela and the deep guitarrón — and every player sings. Migration to Guadalajara and national cultural policy in the 19th and 20th centuries made it a symbol of Mexico.
Q4789767: The Argungu Fishing Festival is a four-day fishing and cultural festival in Argungu, Kebbi State, in north-western Nigeria. Its centrepiece is a contest in which fishermen from across the country try to land the biggest fish from the Sokoto River.
Q483236: Nowruz, meaning ‘new day’, is the Iranian New Year, falling on the spring equinox — usually between 19 and 22 March. Rooted in Zoroastrian tradition and observed for more than 3,000 years, it is now celebrated across West, Central and South Asia, the Caucasus, the Black Sea region and the Balkans, mostly as a secular holiday.
Q4907310: Bikaneri bhujia is a crisp snack from Bikaner in Rajasthan, made from moth-bean and gram flour with spices. Light yellow and similar to sev, it is crunchier and more strongly flavoured. Made largely as a cottage industry, it gives work to many people in the region's villages, especially women.
Q4929641: Jaipur's blue pottery is a craft of Central Asian origin, named for the cobalt-blue dye used to colour it. Strongly influenced by Persian ceramics, it has developed its own designs — animals, birds and flowers with touches of Persian geometry — and some pieces are semi-transparent.
Q5221455: The scissors dance (Danza de las tijeras) is a dance of Chanka origin from the southern Andes of Peru. Two or more dancers, each with their own violin and harp players, take turns performing ever more daring steps — some danced on a single foot. It is strongest in Huancavelica, Ayacucho, Junín, Apurímac and Lima.
Q5269691: Dhokra is metal casting by the lost-wax method, a technique used in India for more than 4,000 years — the bronze dancing girl of Mohenjo-daro is among the earliest known lost-wax objects. Dhokra artisans make horses, elephants, peacocks, owls, religious images, measuring bowls and lamps, prized for their simple, forceful folk forms.
Q54874526: Jirtig is a group of rituals performed mainly at weddings, and less often at boys' circumcisions, in central and northern Sudan along the Nile. Rooted in ancient Sudanese tradition, its rites are meant to protect the couple and bring fertility and abundance. It is especially popular among Nubian peoples such as the Danagla, Ja'aliyin, Rubatab, Manasir and Shaigiya.
Q55607265: The Chhau mask of Purulia in West Bengal is what sets Purulia Chhau apart from the other two styles of the dance, Seraikella and Mayurbhanj. Seraikella dancers wear smaller, simpler masks, while Mayurbhanj dancers wear none; Purulia’s masks are large and vivid.
Q5637073: Hachinohe Sansha Taisai is a festival held from 31 July to 4 August in Hachinohe, Aomori Prefecture, centred on three Shinto shrines. Twenty-seven floats and three portable shrines (mikoshi) are carried through the streets. With a history of nearly three centuries, it was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 2004.
Q604820: The Huaconada is a ritual dance of Mito, a village in the central Andes of Peru. On the first three days of each January, masked men called huacones dance in the village centre: some in traditional costume and finely carved masks meant to inspire respect, others in modern dress portraying fear, sadness or mockery, all keeping time to a small drum, the tinya.
Q6080166: Ishidori Matsuri, the ‘stone-bringing festival’, is held in Kuwana, Mie Prefecture, from midnight on the first Saturday of August. Each district of the town has its own richly decorated three-wheeled cart carrying a large taiko drum and gongs, played in a sequence that identifies the district. Over the weekend the carts are pulled to Kasuga Shrine.
Q611735: Vimbuza is a healing dance of the Tumbuka people of northern Malawi, also found among related communities in eastern Zambia and southern Tanzania. The word covers the spirits believed to cause certain illnesses and the drumming, singing and all-night dancing used to identify and calm them. It took its present form in the 19th and early 20th centuries and survived a colonial ban in the 1920s.
Q6362867: Kangra painting is the art of the former Kangra State in Himachal Pradesh, whose rulers patronised it. The style flourished as the Basohli school faded in the mid-18th century, and it became so prolific that Pahari painting as a whole came to be called the Kangra school.
Q6948725: Mysore painting is a classical South Indian style of painting that grew up in and around Mysore in Karnataka under the patronage of the Mysore rulers. Painting in Karnataka goes back to the age of the Ajanta caves, and the Mysore school developed directly from the painting of the Vijayanagara Empire.
Q6948726: Mysore silk is a mulberry silk from Mysore in Karnataka. Silk-making in the region, which had declined after the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire, was revived under Tipu Sultan in the late 18th century. Today it is closely tied to the Karnataka Silk Industries Corporation, whose Mysore factory — founded in 1912 by Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar — weaves silk saris and other garments.
Q6960716: Nakshi kantha is an embroidered quilt, a centuries-old art of the Bengal region — Bangladesh and the Indian states of West Bengal, Tripura and parts of Assam. Made from layers of old cloth and thread, it takes its name from the Bengali word naksha, ‘pattern’. Early kanthas were white, embroidered in red, blue and black.
Q7125238: The Paithani is a handwoven silk sari named after Paithan, near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar in Maharashtra, where it was first made; today the town of Yeola in Nashik district is its largest producer. It is known for borders of oblique square designs and an end-piece (padar) with peacocks, and for kaleidoscope effects created by weaving with one colour lengthwise and another across.
Q718540: Gagaku, ‘elegant music’, is Japan's classical court music and dance. It took its present form in the Heian period, around the 10th century, at the Kyoto imperial palace, and is still performed by the Board of Ceremonies at the Tokyo Imperial Palace. Wind, percussion and string instruments each embellish a shared main melody.
Q7228884: Pootharekulu, ‘coated sheets’ in Telugu, is a sweet from Andhra Pradesh made of wafer-thin sheets of rice starch wrapped around sugar, dry fruits and nuts. It is served at festivals, religious occasions and weddings. It is a cottage industry in the village of Atreyapuram, where hundreds of families depend on making it.
Q725457: Muslin is a plain-woven cotton cloth, made in weights from fine sheers to coarse sheeting. Bengal was its great centre of production, and the finest came from Sonargaon near Dhaka; after Dhaka became the capital of Mughal Bengal, its muslin reached distant markets as far as Central Asia.
Q7289735: Ramman is a religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal Himalayas in Uttarakhand. The best-known form is the masked Ramman of Saloor-Dungra village in Chamoli district, which is performed nowhere else. It is held in the courtyard of the village temple as an offering to the local deity, Bhumiyal Devta.
Q7409001: The Sambalpuri sari is a handwoven ikat (bandha) sari from western Odisha — Sambalpur, Bargarh, Balangir, Boudh and Sonepur districts — in which the warp and weft threads are tie-dyed before weaving. It carries motifs with deep meaning in Odia culture, such as the conch (shankha), wheel (chakra) and flower (phula), often in red, black and white, the colours associated with Lord Jagannath.
Q7460579: Tholu bommalata is the shadow-puppet theatre of Andhra Pradesh, with roots traced as far back as the 3rd century BCE. Its performers belonged to groups of travelling entertainers who moved from village to village through the year, and the art long enjoyed royal patronage. Before radio, film and television, its performances carried the old epics to village audiences.
Q76605: Couscous is a North African dish of small steamed granules of rolled semolina, often served with a stew spooned over it. It is a staple across the Maghreb — in Algeria, Tunisia, Mauritania, Morocco and Libya — and reached French cuisine in the early 20th century.
Q7677467: The Takayama Festivals in Takayama, Gifu Prefecture, date back to the 16th–17th century, a period when the Kanamori family ruled the area. There are two: the spring Sanno Festival on 14–15 April at the Hie Shrine, held to pray for a good harvest, and the autumn festival on 9–10 October at the Sakurayama Hachiman Shrine, held to give thanks.
Q7849923: The Tsuchizaki Shinmei Shrine Festival is held on 20–21 July in Tsuchizaki, the port district of Akita City. Each neighbourhood contributes a float topped with giant figures, and around twenty parade in honour of the Shinmeisha shrine. It became an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1997.
Q8084052: The ʻie tōga is a finely woven mat of great cultural value in Samoa — called a ‘fine mat’ in English, though it is never used as one. Made by women, and prized for the fineness of the weave and the softness and sheen of the fibre, it has an unwoven fringe and a strip of red feathers. Fine mats are exchanged as gifts at chiefly title bestowals, weddings and funerals.
Q846299: Washi is Japanese paper made by hand from the inner bark of the gampi tree, the mitsumata shrub or the paper mulberry (kōzo). It is the paper of origami, calligraphy and ukiyo-e prints, and was once used for clothes, toys, household goods and ritual objects. Because it is tougher than wood-pulp paper, it is often used to repair historic books and artworks.
Q86753817: Kwagh-hir, ‘a thing of magic’, is a performance art of the Tiv people of central Nigeria that became popular in the 1960s. Combining puppetry, masquerade, poetry, music, dance and storytelling, it tells moral tales about the past and present — to teach, entertain and comment on society. It grew from kwagh-alom, the Tiv tradition of family storytelling.
Q882985: Garba is a circle dance from Gujarat, now danced wherever the Gujarati diaspora gathers. It belongs to Navaratri, the nine nights honouring the goddess Amba, and each night of dancing often ends with dandiya raas, a related circle dance in which partners strike sticks together in rhythm.
Q9350: Yoga is a family of physical, mental and spiritual disciplines that arose in ancient India with its own philosophy, aimed at mastering body and mind to reach liberation. It is practised in Hindu, Jain and Buddhist traditions; it may have older roots but is first attested in the early first millennium BCE. Today it is practised worldwide, often chiefly as exercise.
Q979873: The Gion Matsuri is one of Japan's largest festivals, held throughout July in Kyoto around the Yasaka Shrine in the Gion district. A Shinto festival, it began as a rite to purify the city and calm the forces thought to cause disease. It is best known for its two great processions of floats, the Yamaboko Junkō, on 17 and 24 July.
